items.question: Why must the powers of action and the rest be grounded in consciousness?
premises: The powers of action and the rest are founded on the nature of consciousness.
They cannot be connected with an unconscious nature.
No substrate for such powers can be ascertained apart from consciousness.
items.inference: Therefore the powers of action and the rest necessarily belong to consciousness alone.
uncertainties: The exact force of 'adhikā' here may be 'founded on', 'predominant in', or 'characterized by'.
items.plain_english: The powers of action and the rest are grounded in the nature of consciousness, because they cannot belong to anything unconscious, and no separate substrate for them can be established.

items.question: Does the supreme scripture posit a separate substrate for the powers as qualities?
premises: In the scripture of the Supreme Lord, no substrate for the powers is taught.
The powers are not treated as qualities needing an external support.
This differs from the Kanāda school's doctrine of an unseen quality.
items.inference: Therefore the powers are not dependent on any separate substrate in the manner of qualities.
uncertainties: The precise target of 'kāṇādadṛṣṭivat' may be the Vaiśeṣika notion of adṛṣṭa or more generally their quality-substrate model.
items.plain_english: In the scripture of the Supreme Lord, the powers are not said to have any separate substrate, as if they were qualities in the manner taught by the followers of Kaṇāda.

items.question: What follows if the powers of seeing, action, and will are taken as truly separate?
premises: The powers of seeing, action, will, and the rest would be regarded as distinct.
Shiva is affirmed to be one.
A statement that contradicts the unity of Shiva would lack real referent.
items.inference: Therefore treating those powers as truly separate would make the statement 'Shiva is one' empty of reality.
items.plain_english: If the powers of seeing, action, will, and so on were truly separate, then saying 'Shiva is one' would become mere words without any real basis.

items.question: What is the true nature of freedom when it is examined carefully?
premises: Freedom is nothing other than consciousness itself.
When analyzed, freedom appears in relation to many powers.
Those many powers do not alter its essential nature as consciousness.
items.inference: Therefore freedom is consciousness itself, even though analysis distinguishes it into many powers.
items.plain_english: For this reason, freedom is nothing but consciousness itself; and when examined closely, it is seen to unfold into many powers.

items.question: If liberation is the self's shining forth, does knowing a cause-effect relation guarantee liberation?
premises: Liberation is the shining forth of the self.
A mere cause-effect relation does not by itself produce that shining forth.
Knowing such a relation is not identical with liberation.
items.inference: Therefore one should not assume that knowing a cause necessarily brings liberation.
uncertainties: The compound 'kāraṇātkārya' is compressed; the intended contrast is between causal knowledge and liberating recognition.
items.plain_english: Since liberation is the self's own shining forth, there is no reason to think that merely knowing a cause and its effect will automatically bring liberation.

items.question: Is the relation between knowledge and liberation primarily a cause-and-effect relation?
premises: A cause-and-effect relation between knowledge and liberation has been stated.
That relation is not the primary or ultimate one.
If it were primary, the earlier objection would stand.
items.inference: Therefore the objection does not apply, because the causal relation is not primary.
items.plain_english: Although knowledge is sometimes described as the cause of liberation, that is not the primary way to understand their relation; so the objection raised earlier does not hold.

items.question: How can action, though essentially knowledge, appear as varied and visible?
premises: Action is in essence nothing other than knowledge.
In the self it takes on a kind of grossness or outward form.
That outward form makes multiplicity and visibility appear.
items.inference: Therefore the variety seen in action belongs to its manifest form, not to its essential nature.
uncertainties: The imperative 'dṛśyatāṃ' may be read as 'let it be seen' or as a general statement that visibility appears.
items.plain_english: Action is by nature knowledge itself, but as it takes on a grosser form in the self, its variety becomes visible.

items.question: Why are the means within the path of action said to be innumerable?
premises: The means of action include many subordinate means.
These are distinguished as inner and outer.
They further divide into many kinds and subkinds.
items.inference: Therefore the means within the path of action are innumerable.
uncertainties: The sandhi in 'kriyopāye@bhyupāyānāṃ' is compressed; the reading follows the supplied tokenization.
items.plain_english: Within the path of action, the means are divided into inner and outer and then into many further kinds, so they become countless.

items.question: Does the multiplicity of means imply a multiplicity in liberation itself?
premises: Some wise people suspected that different means might produce different liberations.
The previous explanation showed that multiplicity belongs to the means.
Liberation itself is not thereby divided.
items.inference: Therefore the suspicion that liberation differs according to the means is refuted.
items.plain_english: This also removes the doubt some wise people had, that because the means differ, liberation itself might differ.

items.question: Do different causes of liberation make liberation itself different?
premises: Liberation may occur through destruction of impurity and its power or through the fall of concealment.
These are different causal routes.
A single kind of result can arise from different causes, as in the breaking of a pot.
items.inference: Therefore liberation is not different even when its causes differ.
uncertainties: The compound is dense; the contrast is between removal of impurity and cessation of concealment as alternative causal descriptions.
items.plain_english: Even if liberation comes about through different causes, such as the destruction of impurity and its power or the falling away of concealment, liberation itself is not different, just as the breaking of a pot is one kind of event though caused in different ways.

items.question: Where is the threefold nature of penetration authoritatively taught?
premises: The discussion concerns a threefold division.
This division is taught in the scripture called Śrīpūrva.
It is taught by the Supreme Lord in the context of determining penetration.
items.inference: Therefore the threefoldness of penetration has scriptural authority in the Śrīpūrva.
uncertainties: The exact title 'Śrīpūrva' may refer to a specific āgama section or text known by that name.
items.plain_english: This threefold division was taught by the Supreme Lord in the scripture called Śrīpūrva, in the section that determines the nature of penetration.

items.question: What is the śāmbhava penetration as defined in this teaching?
premises: The recipient is not engaged in any conceptual thought.
The awakening comes through the teacher.
The penetration that arises in that state is named śāmbhava.
items.inference: Therefore śāmbhava penetration is the teacher-awakened immersion of one free from conceptual thought.
items.plain_english: When a person who is thinking of nothing at all is awakened by the teacher and penetration arises, that is called the śāmbhava penetration.

items.question: How is the śākta penetration defined in this passage?
premises: The practitioner contemplates a reality without verbal utterance.
This contemplation occurs through the mind alone.
The penetration attained in that way is called śākta.
items.inference: Therefore śākta penetration is the mind-based immersion into a non-verbal reality.
items.plain_english: When one contemplates a reality without utterance, using the mind alone, and attains penetration in that way, it is called the śākta penetration.

items.question: What characterizes the āṇava penetration in this threefold scheme?
premises: This penetration arises through utterance, bodily action, meditation, letters, and imagined loci.
It depends on constructed supports and practices.
Such a penetration is designated āṇava.
items.inference: Therefore āṇava penetration is the immersion attained through constructed ritual and contemplative supports.
uncertainties: The range of 'karaṇa' may include bodily or ritual operations; the gloss keeps it broad.
items.plain_english: The penetration that arises through utterance, bodily practice, meditation, letters, and imagined locations is properly called the āṇava penetration.

items.question: What does the phrase 'thinking of nothing' indicate in the śāmbhava state?
premises: The phrase refers to one who does not employ conceptual construction.
Without conceptual construction, absorption into the knowable occurs suddenly.
This sudden absorption is being explained as the key feature.
items.inference: Therefore 'thinking of nothing' means the suspension of conceptual construction that allows immediate absorption into the knowable.
items.plain_english: The expression 'one who thinks of nothing' means that conceptual construction is not in use, and through that there is a sudden absorption into what is to be known.

items.question: How does that sudden absorption into the knowable come about?
premises: The question asks for the cause of sudden absorption.
The answer points to a most weighty teacher.
That teacher's awareness is turned toward the knowable and is immediately mature.
items.inference: Therefore sudden absorption arises through the powerful, mature, knowable-directed awakening imparted by the teacher.
items.plain_english: How does that happen? It happens through a most weighty teacher, whose awareness is turned toward the knowable and whose awakening is immediately mature.

items.question: How is the grammatical form in the teacher phrase explained, and what is penetration for the dependent self?
premises: The suffix can be explained in the sense of the third case or by difference of reference.
Penetration belongs to the dependent self.
It occurs through immersion into its own form and into that higher form.
items.inference: Therefore the verse offers a grammatical clarification and defines penetration as the dependent self's immersion into its true form.
uncertainties: The grammatical note is terse; the exact syntactic target in the prior verse is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: The verse gives a grammatical explanation of the earlier expression and adds that, for the dependent self, penetration means sinking into its own true form.

items.question: What is the intended meaning of the statement about penetration in this context?
premises: Penetration involves becoming of the nature of the supreme.
Shambhu is primal and not divided from his power.
The meaning of the statement is meant to shine forth by itself.
items.inference: Therefore the statement means self-manifest identity with Shambhu, who is inseparable from his power.
items.plain_english: The meaning here is that one comes to share the nature of Shambhu, the primal Lord who is never separate from his power; this meaning is to be understood as shining forth on its own.

items.question: How does the knowable manifest in the śāmbhava awakening without conceptual determination?
premises: The manifestation occurs even without determinate judgment.
It appears suddenly, reflected in the mirror of the subject.
It overpowers the subject and displays its own majesty.
items.inference: Therefore in śāmbhava awakening the knowable reveals itself directly, overwhelming the subject without conceptual mediation.
uncertainties: The metaphor of the subject as mirror is compact; the gloss preserves the image rather than paraphrasing it away.
items.plain_english: Even without any determinate judgment, it suddenly appears reflected in the mirror of the subject, overwhelms the subject, and displays its own majesty.

items.question: How is the knowable classified in relation to degrees of purity of heart?
premises: The knowable abides according to degrees of purity of heart.
It is divided into two kinds.
One is mere consciousness and the other is inert and constructed.
items.inference: Therefore the knowable appears either as pure consciousness or as inert constructed object, depending on the heart's purity.
uncertainties: The phrase 'ādyaṃ ca kalpitam' is slightly compressed; the reading takes the first as consciousness and the other as constructed.
items.plain_english: Depending on the degree of purity of the heart, the knowable appears in two ways: as mere consciousness, or as something inert and constructed.

items.question: What kind of penetration occurs when the knowable appears as inert?
premises: The other kind of knowable is treated as real in its own way.
A division is made between penetrations based on the knowable.
Penetration with the inert takes the form of a reflected image.
items.inference: Therefore immersion into the inert knowable is a reflective, image-like penetration rather than identity with pure consciousness.
uncertainties: The phrase 'itarattu tathā satyaṃ' is brief; it may mean the other is also real in appearance or in its own domain.
items.plain_english: The other kind of knowable is also treated as real in its own way; penetration into what is inert takes the form of a reflected image.

items.question: What is the nature of penetration when it occurs with pure consciousness?
premises: Penetration with consciousness is nothing other than identity.
Such identity does not rely on constructed supports.
Therefore the awareness involved is non-conceptual and independent of contemplative techniques.
items.inference: Therefore penetration into consciousness is direct identity, realized as non-conceptual awareness.
items.plain_english: Penetration into consciousness is nothing other than identity with it; for that reason the awareness involved is non-conceptual and does not depend on contemplation or similar practices.

items.question: What is śāmbhava penetration and what role do later determinations play in it?
premises: Śāmbhava penetration is identity with Shiva.
By its grace, determinate understandings may arise afterward.
Those later understandings follow the penetration rather than produce it.
items.inference: Therefore śāmbhava penetration is primary identity with Shiva, and subsequent determinations are secondary effects of its grace.
items.plain_english: Here śāmbhava penetration is the attainment of identity with Shiva; any determinate understandings that arise afterward come by its grace, not as its cause.

items.question: Can later determinate understandings function as the means to śāmbhava penetration?
premises: Later determinations may be in harmony with the attained identity.
They still depend on conceptual construction.
Valid cognition in this context is said to be non-conceptual.
items.inference: Therefore later determinations cannot be the means to śāmbhava penetration, even if they accord with it.
uncertainties: The final participle 'bruvan' may refer to the text's authorial voice or to a general doctrinal statement.
items.plain_english: Even if later determinate understandings arise in harmony with that identity, they cannot be its means, because they depend on conceptual construction, while the valid cognition in question is non-conceptual.
